passage:
12 November
Irfan forgot my birthday. Completely. No call, no message, nothing, and then he posted photos from a cricket match that evening. My first thought at 11 p.m. was: he never really cared. Classic Irfan, always about himself.
Then I made myself write the other list. Irfan drove three hours to help me move flats in the rain. He sat with me in the hospital when Papa had his operation. He lent me money without asking when I'd pay it back.
Both lists are true. He's caring and he's careless. Those aren't opposites; they're just two facts about one person. I don't have to erase the first list because of the second.
So tomorrow I'll call and tell him it stung. Not a verdict on our whole friendship, just one thing that hurt.
Abhinav

qa.q: What did Irfan post on the evening of the birthday?
qa.a: Photos from a cricket match.

qa.q: Why did 'he never really cared' feel true to Abhinav at 11 p.m.?
qa.a: The hurt of being forgotten was fresh and strong, so for that moment one careless act seemed to define the whole friendship.

qa.q: Which choice helped Abhinav keep the friendship steady?
qa.a: Writing the second list of Irfan's kindnesses and deciding to call about one thing that stung, instead of judging the whole friendship.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel when Abhinav calls tomorrow?
qa.a: Probably embarrassed and sorry about forgetting, and relieved that Abhinav raised it as one hurt rather than ending things.

grounding: An adult hurt by a friend's forgotten birthday reminds themselves that the friend is both caring and careless, and plans a calm conversation instead of a verdict.

passage:
In the kasba of Nabha, Kiran and Salma ran a small tailoring shop together above the sweet shop. On Monday morning Kiran found the door unlocked and two bolts of wedding silk gone. Salma had forgotten to lock up again.
Kiran's first thought, standing in the empty doorway, was hot and total: she's useless, she's always been careless, I should never have trusted her. Then she sat on the step and made herself remember. Salma had sat up three nights with Kiran's baby during the fever. Salma had taught her to cut blouse patterns for nothing. Salma was kind, and Salma was careless. Both.
When Salma arrived, pale, Kiran said, "I'm very angry about the silk. I'm not angry about you. From now on, I lock up." Salma cried, and then they walked to the police station together.

qa.q: What was missing from the shop on Monday morning?
qa.a: Two bolts of wedding silk.

qa.q: Why did 'she's useless' feel so true to Kiran in the doorway?
qa.a: The loss was sudden and costly, so her anger made one careless act feel like the whole truth about Salma.

qa.q: Which choice helped Kiran respond without breaking the partnership?
qa.a: Remembering Salma's kindness on the step, then separating her anger about the silk from her view of Salma, and taking over the locking up herself.

qa.q: What might Salma have feared as she arrived at the shop?
qa.a: That Kiran would end their partnership or friendship; hearing 'I'm not angry about you' likely brought huge relief along with guilt.

grounding: A woman whose business partner's carelessness cost them stock reminds herself the partner is also deeply kind, and responds without an explosion.

passage:
The last train into Porto arrived at midnight, and Tariq had promised to pick Rosa up. She stood under the station awning for forty minutes, rain dripping off the edge, calling a phone that went to voicemail.
In the taxi home the old voice started: He doesn't care. He never did. She caught it. That wasn't true either. In March, Tariq had sat with her in the emergency room for six hours when she broke her wrist. He'd learned to make her grandmother's soup.
Rosa said it to herself slowly, like a sum: Tariq is caring. Tariq was careless tonight. Both are real.
In the morning he appeared at her door, grey-faced. "I fell asleep on the sofa. I'm so sorry."
"I was really upset," Rosa said. "I still am, a bit. And I know you care. Can you set an alarm next time?"
He nodded, and they made coffee.

qa.q: How long did Rosa wait under the station awning?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: Why did "He doesn't care. He never did" feel true to Rosa in the taxi?
qa.a: She was cold, tired and hurt after waiting in the rain, and in that disappointment one careless night seemed to wipe out everything good.

qa.q: What choice in the taxi kept the disappointment from exploding?
qa.a: Rosa remembered the emergency room and the soup and held both facts, caring and careless, so she could say she was upset and ask for an alarm without calling the friendship a lie.

qa.q: What might it be like for Tariq to hear "And I know you care"?
qa.a: Tariq, grey-faced and ashamed, would probably feel relieved that the mistake was named honestly without being treated as proof that he didn't care.

grounding: Shows an adult who, after being let down, tells herself a friend is both caring and careless, which keeps her disappointment honest but steady.

In the staffroom of the Pune school where they both taught Class 7, Zainab found out at eight: the unit-test marks she'd handed Aditi to upload had never reached the office. The principal wanted to know why Zainab's section had no marks.
Her first thought was sharp: Aditi always does this. Only helps when it suits. Then Zainab looked at the grey cardigan on her own chair, Aditi's cardigan, lent last week when Zainab had fever and Aditi had quietly taken her classes for two days.
Both, she told herself. Aditi is generous, and Aditi is disorganised. One doesn't cancel the other.
At break she said, "Aditi, the marks didn't go in, and the principal questioned me. That was stressful."
Aditi's hand flew to cover a gasp. "Oh no. It's still on my pen drive."
"Can you send it now? And let's keep a checklist for uploads."
The marks went in by lunch. The cardigan went back with a thank-you note.

qa.q: What had Aditi lent Zainab last week?
qa.a: Aditi's grey cardigan, when Zainab had fever.

qa.q: Why did "Aditi always does this" come to Zainab's mind first?
qa.a: Being questioned by the principal made her anxious and stung, and in that moment one careless mistake seemed to define Aditi completely.

qa.q: How did holding both facts shape what Zainab said at break?
qa.a: She named the problem and the stress plainly without attacking Aditi's character, then asked for the file and a checklist, which fixed things by lunch.

qa.q: How might Aditi feel being told calmly instead of blamed?
qa.a: Aditi probably felt embarrassed but safe enough to own the mistake straight away, instead of getting defensive.

grounding: Illustrates an adult who keeps in view that a colleague is both generous and careless, so a mistake leads to a calm fix rather than an explosion.

passage:
Harsha,

I've been angry for a week, and I want to write this before I say something I'll regret.

You forgot my graduation dinner. I kept a chair for you all evening. I told myself you just don't care, that you've never cared, that I've been the only one trying.

And then I remembered last winter. When I had dengue, you drove four hours from Nashik, slept on my floor for three nights and made me that terrible khichdi.

Both of those are you. The friend who drove four hours, and the friend who forgot the dinner. I don't have to pick one. You can be caring and careless. So can I, honestly.

I'm still a bit hurt. But I'm not going to throw away the four hours because of one missed dinner.

Coffee on Sunday?

Kamal

qa.q: How far did Harsha drive when Kamal had dengue?
qa.a: Four hours, from Nashik.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel after remembering last winter?
qa.a: Kamal still felt hurt, but remembering Harsha's care made the anger less explosive and the disappointment easier to hold.

qa.q: What makes Kamal's letter a steadier way to handle disappointment?
qa.a: It names the hurt honestly while keeping Harsha's caring side in view, so the friendship isn't thrown away over one mistake.

qa.q: How might Harsha feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Harsha might feel guilty about the dinner but also relieved and grateful that Kamal still sees the whole friendship.

grounding: Shows an adult telling themselves that a friend can be caring and careless, keeping both in view so the disappointment is less explosive.

passage: Nandini, you asked how I stopped fighting with my mother every week. Let me, Sahil, explain. For years I saw her in two ways. When she was kind, she was a saint. When she forgot something, she was the worst mother alive. Like the night she forgot to pick me up from the station at midnight, and I waited two hours. I didn't speak to her for a week. But the same woman sat by my bed for eleven nights when I had typhoid in class nine, wiping my forehead. Both are true. She's caring and she's careless. Once I let myself hold both, something changed. When she forgets now, I'm annoyed, and I tell her. But it doesn't feel like the end of the world. It's just her careless side. Her caring side is still there, right next to it.

qa.q: How long did Sahil wait at the station?
qa.a: Two hours.

qa.q: Why does Sahil feel less upset now when his mother forgets something?
qa.a: Sahil holds both her careless and caring sides in mind, so a lapse feels annoying, not like a betrayal that erases everything good.

qa.q: What could Nandini take from Sahil's story for her own relationships?
qa.a: That she can admit someone's flaws and their care together, and speak up about the flaw without deciding the whole person is bad.

qa.q: How might Sahil's mother experience the change in him?
qa.a: She might feel relieved and closer to him, hearing honest complaints instead of weeks of silence.

grounding: Shows an adult learning to see a parent as both caring and careless, making the relationship steadier and disappointment less explosive.

passage: I share a flat with Ayesha in Hyderabad, and I saw how she handled Chinmay missing her award ceremony. I can only say what I saw. He'd promised to come. The seat next to her stayed empty. She came home with the trophy, sat on the sofa, and was quiet for a long time. I expected her to call him and end it. She'd done that before, with others. Instead she said, half to me and half to herself, "He's the one who stayed up all night helping me with the application. He's also the one who forgot tonight. Both are Chinmay." Then she called him. I heard her say, calmly, "I'm really hurt you weren't there. I needed you tonight." She didn't shout. She didn't say it was over. The next morning, he turned up with breakfast and an apology.

qa.q: What did Chinmay help Ayesha with?
qa.a: He stayed up all night helping her with the application.

qa.q: Why didn't Ayesha end things with Chinmay, as the narrator expected?
qa.a: Ayesha felt hurt and disappointed, but holding in mind both his help with the application and his forgetfulness kept the disappointment from exploding.

qa.q: What makes Ayesha's phone call a good response?
qa.a: She named her hurt clearly and calmly, without shouting or ending things, which invited Chinmay to take responsibility.

qa.q: How might Chinmay have felt hearing Ayesha's calm words?
qa.a: Chinmay likely felt guilty and grateful for the chance to make it right, which is why he came with breakfast and an apology.

grounding: Shows, through a flatmate's account, an adult holding that her partner is both caring and careless, keeping disappointment steady.

passage:
Before, Monday: Maria's flight landed at 11 p.m. Divyansh had promised to pick her up. He didn't come; he'd fallen asleep. She took a taxi home, furious, typing "You never think about anyone but yourself" and not sending it.

During, Tuesday: in the morning she found the soup he'd brought her last month still in her freezer, labelled "for sick days, M". She remembered the week he'd sat with her through a fever. She wrote on a sticky note: Divyansh is caring. Divyansh is careless. Both true.

After, Friday: when they met, she didn't explode and didn't pretend. "Monday really hurt. I needed you there, and you forgot." He winced. "I'm sorry. I'll set two alarms next time." "And I know you care," she said. "That's why it stung." They were both calmer than she'd expected.

qa.q: What time did Maria's flight land?
qa.a: Maria's flight landed at 11 p.m.

qa.q: Why did Maria write "Both true" on the sticky note?
qa.a: Maria was hurt and angry about Monday but also grateful for the fever week, and holding both helped her calm down instead of writing Divyansh off.

qa.q: Which choice on Friday worked, and why?
qa.a: Maria named the hurt clearly without exploding and also said she knew he cared, so Divyansh could apologise and plan two alarms.

qa.q: How might Divyansh feel hearing "That's why it stung"?
qa.a: Divyansh likely feels sorry but also reassured that one mistake hasn't erased his care.

grounding: Over a week a woman let down by Divyansh reminds herself he is both caring and careless, so her disappointment stays steady.

passage:
Lokesh, you're furious with your friend for forgetting your birthday. Let your Binita Nani tell you about my brother Tapan. When my first baby came, Tapan drove through the night from Siliguri with a box of mangoes and sat with me for three days. That was Tapan. And the same Tapan missed my wedding reception because he was watching a football final. Also Tapan.

For years I kept flipping. Some days he was a saint; other days I swore I'd never speak to him again. It was exhausting, like a see-saw.

Then my mother told me, "Binu, he is both. Hold both in your hands." So I did. When he forgot things, I told him straight: "That hurt." And I still ate his mangoes. We never had a big explosion again. He died last year, and I miss both of him.

qa.q: What did Tapan bring when Binita's first baby came?
qa.a: Tapan brought a box of mangoes.

qa.q: What was young Binita feeling in the years of flipping about Tapan?
qa.a: Young Binita felt torn and exhausted, swinging between seeing him as a saint and never wanting to speak to him.

qa.q: What turning point in the story steadied things?
qa.a: Her mother's words "he is both, hold both" led Binita to name hurts directly while still valuing his care.

qa.q: How might Tapan have experienced Binita's straight "That hurt"?
qa.a: Tapan probably found it easier to hear than silence or explosions, and could say sorry while staying close.

grounding: A grandmother recalls learning to see her brother as both caring and careless, which ended years of swinging between praise and fury.

passage:
The power had been out for two hours, Pooja's interview was at nine the next morning, and her phone was at nine percent because Yamini had borrowed the power bank and left it at the office. Again.

Pooja stood in the dark kitchen, heat rising in her chest. The old speech started in her head: Yamini is selfish, Yamini never thinks, why do I even live with her.

Then her phone torch lit the fridge door. Taped there was Yamini's list from last week: "Pooja's interview prep: 1. mock questions 2. iron the blue kurta 3. make her eat breakfast." Yamini had quizzed her for two evenings.

Pooja breathed out. Caring and careless. Same person. When Yamini came home at ten, Pooja said, "I'm upset about the power bank. I really needed it tonight." Yamini's face fell. "Oh no. Take my phone for the alarm."

qa.q: Where did Yamini leave the power bank?
qa.a: Yamini left the power bank at the office.

qa.q: Why did Pooja feel her anger settle in the dark kitchen?
qa.a: Seeing Yamini's interview-prep list reminded Pooja of the care alongside the carelessness, so the heat in her chest eased and she felt calmer.

qa.q: What did Pooja do well when Yamini came home?
qa.a: Pooja named the specific upset about the power bank without calling Yamini selfish, which let Yamini respond helpfully.

qa.q: How might Yamini feel hearing Pooja's words?
qa.a: Yamini seems sorry and eager to fix it, perhaps relieved that Pooja spoke calmly rather than exploding.

grounding: Shows a young woman, the night before an interview, holding in mind that her flatmate is both caring and careless.

passage: Lakshmi waited forty minutes at Ernakulam station in the rain, phone dead, before taking an auto home. Jomon had forgotten. Again. On the ride, her mind started its old swing: he doesn't care, he never did. Then she stopped herself and did what she had been practising. She said quietly, under her breath, "Jomon is caring. Jomon is also careless." She made herself list both. Caring: he had sat up with her through her father's surgery; he remembered her mother's medicines. Careless: the station, twice now. Both were real. When she got home and he rushed to the door, apologising, she didn't explode or pretend it was fine. "I'm hurt," she said. "And I know you love me. Can we set up a reminder system?"

qa.q: How long did Lakshmi wait at the station?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What swing did Lakshmi's mind start on the auto ride?
qa.a: A hurt, angry swing toward "he doesn't care, he never did".

qa.q: What did Lakshmi do to hold both truths?
qa.a: She said aloud that Jomon is caring and also careless, listed examples of both, then told him she was hurt while asking for a reminder system.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel at the door?
qa.a: Guilty and anxious, rushing to apologise, and relieved that she didn't explode.

grounding: An adult reminds herself a person can be both caring and careless, and responds steadily instead of swinging to all bad.

passage:
"Papa missed my graduation, Nitin. He said he'd be there."
"I know. He mixed up the date."
"Last week I'd have said he's the best father in the world. Today I want to say he's the worst."
"Which one is true?"
Kashish sighed. "Neither. Both? He drove me to every exam for three years. He also forgets things that matter to me."
"That sounds like Papa."
"I'm trying to hold both. Caring and careless. It's harder than picking one."
"Picking one is easier for about a day."
"Then it explodes."
"Exactly. So what will you tell him?"
"That I'm hurt. And that I know he loves me. Both."

qa.q: What did Papa do for three years?
qa.a: Drove Kashish to every exam.

qa.q: What does Kashish feel today about Papa?
qa.a: Hurt and angry enough to want to call him the worst father, while knowing that isn't the whole truth.

qa.q: What does Kashish plan to tell Papa?
qa.a: That Kashish is hurt, and knows he loves them: both truths together.

qa.q: How does Nitin help?
qa.a: Nitin asks which one is true and agrees that picking one explodes later, helping Kashish hold both.

grounding: An adult holds that a father is both caring and careless, and plans to say both instead of swinging to one.

passage: For years, my friendship with Nikita swung like a pendulum. When she remembered my birthday with a handmade card, she was my soulmate. When she cancelled on me twice in a month, she was selfish and I'd think about ending it. Last year a friend asked me, "Is she good or bad?" and I realised the question itself was the problem. Nikita is generous, and she is disorganised. She's loyal, and she forgets plans. Both are simply true. Now, when she cancels, I say, "That's annoying, and I still love you." I also book our plans for weekends, when she's less stretched. I'm Vinita, and our friendship is calmer than it has ever been.

qa.q: What did Nikita make for Vinita's birthday?
qa.a: A handmade card.

qa.q: How did Vinita use to feel when Nikita cancelled?
qa.a: Hurt and angry enough to think Nikita was selfish and to consider ending the friendship.

qa.q: What does Vinita do now?
qa.a: Holds both truths, says "That's annoying, and I still love you", and books plans for weekends when Nikita is less stretched.

qa.q: How might Nikita experience the calmer friendship?
qa.a: More relaxed and secure, no longer swinging between soulmate and selfish in Vinita's eyes.

grounding: An adult learns to see a friend as both generous and disorganised, which makes the friendship steadier.

passage:
Session note, Thursday.
Ishita arrived calmer than last month. Her brother Divyansh forgot to collect her after her minor surgery on Saturday; she waited ninety minutes at the hospital gate. In March, she told me, a similar lapse led her to block his number for a week.
This time she described it differently. "He's the one who sat with Amma every night when she was ill. And he forgot me on Saturday. Both are true. I'm allowed to be annoyed, and he's still my brother." She said she told him plainly that the wait hurt; he apologised and cooked dinner for her twice this week.
I pointed out how much steadier this felt than March. Next: we will practise the same both-and phrasing for her conflicts at work.

qa.q: How long did Ishita wait at the hospital gate?
qa.a: Ninety minutes.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling about Divyansh this time?
qa.a: She felt annoyed and hurt about the wait but still affectionate, keeping both his care for Amma and his lapse in view.

qa.q: What does the counsellor plan next, and why?
qa.a: Practising the same both-and phrasing for conflicts at work, because keeping both sides in view made Ishita's reaction steadier than in March.

qa.q: How might Divyansh have experienced the difference from March?
qa.a: Instead of being blocked for a week, he heard plainly that the wait hurt, which gave him the chance to apologise and make amends by cooking dinner.

grounding: An adult tells herself her brother is both caring and careless, and her disappointment stays steady instead of explosive.
